source.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Emotion Control in Text-to-Speech
source.authors: Hong-Fei Du; Jia-Cheng Shi; Sidi Lu; Gang Zhou; Ye Gao

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends SAE feature analysis to autoregressive TTS semantic backbones and reports results on sparse, emotion-related features and their interventions. It is not a reproduction of the toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: Results on TTS baseline systems, human ratings, WER, speaker similarity, and general steering performance are not recorded unless they directly measure selected SAE-feature effects. The suppression portion of Table 1 is flattened ambiguously, so its values are not assigned to conditions. Figure-only values without a textual description are not recorded as numeric results.
record.test_reason: Mostly a steering-method paper. It does report SAE-recovered sparse, emotion-selective features in a new setting, the IndexTTS2 semantic backbone: reconstruction, selectivity distributions and causal single-feature effects. These bear weakly on V4. Its one dictionary-size comparison bears on V5. Table 1/3 and LLaSA steering scores are method performance (T4-like), not tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim that steering the selected sparse features matches or beats global mean-difference steering and TTS baselines on emotion induction and suppression, while largely preserving content, naturalness and speaker identity.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains k-sparse autoencoders on TTS semantic-backbone activations and intervenes on selected SAE features; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition experiments or their geometric transition analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE latent dimensionality changes feature fragmentation and interpretability (4,096 versus 10,240); emotion control varies with feature budget (top-1, top-3, top-6) and emotion; selection criterion changes alignment; steering scale changes emotion alignment.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The full analysis is conducted on one primary backbone configuration; the authors describe the cross-backbone analysis as additional. The larger SAE dimension comparison is qualitative, and the paper does not test feature stability across runs or SAE methods. Some plotted findings have no exact values in the text, and Table 1's suppression values are flattened ambiguously.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 suppression values were left out because the flattened layout does not reliably assign the reported numbers to methods, emotions, and metrics. Figure-only scale-sweep values without a textual numeric description were not transcribed. TTS baselines and human-rating results were left out because they do not directly measure the SAE feature representation.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry.
All: no test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions.
Spread of features across neurons. General text LLMs. Any baseline (e.g. random-init or neuron basis) against which SAE recovery is compared.
Completeness, stability across seeds or SAE methods, quantitative splitting analysis.
All: no comparison of 1-D directions vs multidimensional features.

missing.what: Feature-budget result: happiness is steerable with a single top-1 feature, while anger and sadness need top-3/top-6 (described as more distributed). Qualitative only.
Single feature #24 shifts spectral centroid monotonically with steering scale from -60 to +60 (20 utterances, 95% CIs).

record.verdict_notes: Superposition is only assumed: the paper cites Elhage et al. as motivation for SAEs and never tests it. Most rows were method-performance results and are relinked to none. The V4 support rests on standard SAE-quality and interpretability evidence in one TTS backbone, with no comparison against neuron-basis or random-model baselines.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature count relative to network dimension, a sparsity-dependent superposition transition, and regular geometric arrangements.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by competition for network capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study tests SAE-recoverable sparse features in TTS semantic backbones, not feature spread across neurons in general LLMs or the prevalence of such features across a broad range of LLMs.
The study tests sensitivity to SAE latent dimensionality, but does not establish feature completeness, stability across training runs or SAE methods, or canonicality across representations.
The study uses one decoder direction per SAE latent feature but does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features or test which geometry is intrinsic to the model.

rows.subject: IndexTTS2

rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE latent-space dimensionalities and assessed resulting feature fragmentation and interpretability.
rows.measure: Reconstruction error and emotion-related feature organization
rows.value: The 10,240-dimensional SAE had lower reconstruction error, but emotion-related features became more fragmented and distributed across more sparse directions, reducing interpretability
rows.note: This tests feature organization's sensitivity to dictionary dimensionality; no numerical reconstruction errors are given for the comparison.

rows.subject: IndexTTS2
rows.stage_stated: autoregressive semantic backbone; layer-16 pre-LayerNorm residual stream
rows.operation_detail: Steered one selected happiness-related SAE latent feature in matched neutral text-speaker conditions.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity to the target-emotion prototype in emotion2vec space
rows.baseline: zero-scale neutral condition; real neutral and happiness reference levels
rows.value: Similarity increases smoothly with the steering scale, from approximately 0.77 at -60 to 0.86 at +60

source_check.correct: Appendix D.1 reports a fixed selected emotion-related latent feature, without identifying its emotion or rank. Figure 9 identifies the zero-scale condition as the neutral baseline and shows 95% confidence intervals. The rank-1 happiness feature, three scales {−60, 0, +60}, and real neutral/happiness reference levels belong to Section 4.2.2 and Figure 6.

relationships.condition: IndexTTS2 semantic backbone, layer-16 residual, 4,096-latent Top-32 SAE
relationships.reason: The SAE reconstructs with normalized MSE 0.129 (r1). A small sparse tail of emotion-selective features appears for each emotion (r3-r5). Steering single features shifts emotion similarity, F0 and energy (r9-r11). Weak evidence: there are no baselines for SAE feature recovery.
relationships.display_finding: The SAE reached normalized MSE 0.129 and showed a small sparse tail of emotion-selective features per emotion; steering single features shifted emotion similarity, F0 and energy. The evidence is weak, with no baselines for feature recovery.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: IndexTTS2 semantic backbone, layer-16 residual, 4,096-latent Top-32 SAE
source_check.reason: Reconstruction, emotion-selective activation distributions, and causal single-feature effects support SAE-recoverable structure in this setting. Top-k sparsity alone does not establish semantic recovery, and r9 requires correction of its feature identity.

relationships.reason: Moving to the larger SAE fragmented emotion features across more directions while lowering reconstruction error. The organisation of features thus depends on dictionary size; the evidence is qualitative (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Going from 4,096 to 10,240 latents lowered reconstruction error but spread emotion features over more directions, qualitative evidence that feature organisation depends on dictionary size.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Appendix B explicitly reports lower reconstruction error but greater fragmentation of emotion-related features in the larger dictionary, qualitatively demonstrating dependence on dictionary size.
